My name is Quinton and I'm 23. I live in Halifax, Nova Scotia. I was born here, but my parents are from France. Quinton was an amazing baby, it was probably his easiest delivery. I was always playing different sports, but I think the one sport I stuck with till now is soccer. I was always like an outdoorsy kid. This is me trying to do a backflip. It didn't end so well. He actually presented a couple of science fair projects and then he was selected to go to the national level, so he went to Ottawa.

I was in grade 8 at the time. I won a bronze medal in science and mathematics and then an award in astronomy. I like math because I like to problem-solve and I think having a set of conditions and trying to find a solution to those conditions is pretty cool. By grade 11, everything was on track. I had really good grades and I had great friends.

My dad decided to take a sabbatical for seven months, so our family was living in Mexico. We were having a great time, I was learning about the culture, the history and the land. I was enrolled in a high school there and learning Spanish. I was also doing courses from Canada, in an International Baccalaureate program.

It's really a higher level than just regular high school, so that actually put pressure on any kid who does that program. But I think what really pushed it over the edge is that I was actually doing two high school programs at the same time, one in Mexico and one back in Halifax. I could feel a bit of the tension building.

I had this big essay that was on my plate and I wasn't moving along, I was really struggling with it. And I think I just cracked. I just couldn't take the stress anymore, and that's probably where the psychotic episode came from. It was very gradual at first. I noticed very small changes in my environment.

For example, I would see a red car outside just going down the street. And then for some reason I would see a red flower and I would try to connect the dots. I thought that seeing the color red twice represented red blood, and that meant someone in my family was going to die. Over the course of several weeks, it really got worse.

A lot of people would describe it as a really bad trip. I can't compare it with drugs, but it's probably worse than any trip you can have. You think the aliens are there, you think the police is out to get you. All these thoughts are very scary and they don't make a lot of sense to other people, but for me they made sense.

My parents did the most they could, but they had no idea what was going on. Quinton was making less and less sense. He was a different person. He was completely restless, up and down, up and down. He must have been 16 or 17. There is also the possibility that maybe this is just a phase, sort of a teenage phase.

I was completely living inside my own head. I was walking down a beach and my father was walking and I thought I had to walk in his footsteps in order to avoid the sun to protect him. The number one feeling I went through was fear. The diving trip was what caused my parents to realize I needed help.

My mother was my diving partner. This photo was the last photo taken before I had a complete breakdown. I remember being underwater and seeing all these fish and the way they moved was very hypnotic. I wanted to touch them because I thought maybe I would get some kind of superpower from them.

This is probably the most vivid part of my memories. I went straight to the surface, which is something you shouldn't do. All of a sudden he went up. You need to tell everybody there's something wrong. I got in the ship and I wasn't even talking to anyone, I was just in my own world.

Complete silence on the boat. He didn't talk to me. I tried to engage him. He was looking up, looking down, completely no Quinton. I kind of started to cry. You don't know if you've lost him forever. When this happened, we went back in town and I managed to get an appointment with a psychiatrist pretty quickly.
When I saw the psychiatrist, they very quickly realized I was having a psychotic episode. They gave me medication immediately.

Quinton is a patient of the Nova Scotia Early Psychosis Program. Early intervention in psychosis and schizophrenia is very important, not only to get control of the symptoms, but really trying to maximize those long-term outcomes for that person with as minimal disruption as possible.

They told my parents that it would take time to start working. We had to keep an eye on him, keep the window closed. The doctor said, don't let him approach any window. In this state, he might just walk out and jump because maybe he thinks that he can fly. Disoriented, very paranoid, very delusional. I could have done something really bad.

Three things that were crucial in my recovery were medication, family and friend support, and having a good medical team.

This video models how a clinician can ask about these things in a structured and evidence-based way, even in the context of a routine clinical appointment. The questionnaire being used is called the ACE, or the Adverse Childhood Experiences Questionnaire. It's a 10-item tool that asks about childhood experiences such as sexual, physical, or verbal abuse, physical neglect, and emotional deprivation. It also asks if a child has experienced parent loss due to incarceration or divorce, major mental illness or substance use in a parent, and domestic violence. For each endorsed item, the child gets one point, called their ACE score. We screen for these because a large body of literature links these events with long-term serious physical and mental health outcomes. Higher scores increase the risk of cardiovascular disease, stroke, diabetes, depression, substance use, and suicide. I think my wife's gonna like that one because she likes it as I'm working on this stuff. I'm sure she'll like it, though. It's tough, it's not easy, but I know it's worth it.

I'm determined because I don't like how I felt after betraying my mother or the physical experience of vomiting. Even if I do drink, I don't want to drink to the point where that happens. It's not worth it.
What do you think is a realistic goal for you then?
To focus on my studies first and regain trust with my mother. If I go to a party, I don't have to drink, or at most have one cup, but I'd prefer not to do that at all.
So your goal is to not drink at all, or if you are at a party, a maximum of one.
Exactly, just so I can take part in the social convention without overdoing it.

Chris, I really appreciate you talking with me. I care about you as a student and athlete and want what's best for you. It seems like you have a good plan, striving not to drink or limiting yourself to one maximum.
Thank you for listening to me. It means a lot.
It's my pleasure, it's the part of the job I like best. Now you better hurry up and get changed for practice.

I mean, it was just like a social gathering, it wasn't like I was looking for it. Yeah, I understand exactly what you're saying and...

Every other weekend, I would say.
Tommy, I'm just so concerned. You know, can't you think of anything better to do?

Are your friends the problem? Maybe you should just start hanging out with more kids in the youth group and not hang out with those kids you were partying with.

Yeah, I guess I haven't really put it on myself, I guess it's really been forced on their account and I've just been following in their footsteps just because it seems like what they're doing is a lot of fun and I just want to make sure I'm getting every bit of the high school experience that I can.

Well there's a lot of things that seem fun in the moment that we know aren't a good choice, right? That's some of the things we talk about all the time is making good choices for our life and really doing what's best for you and I just... you know, I really think you should think about making a big change here.

Yeah, I do see that maybe me drinking not as much would possibly better my life to a certain degree and it does make a lot of sense and I guess I can put more effort into sort of lowering the level of drinking that I...
I think you really need to quit.

Yeah, I mean alcohol is just so prevalent in our society and it's just around me wherever I go in parties and stuff that I kind of feel like I should just get used to it or at least understand its effects before I should let it get out of my life entirely. I don't really see it as something that will completely destroy my life.

I think you're wrong. You know, it really worries me. Anyway, I wish you would quit. If all you're going to do is cut down, that's better than nothing. You know, I appreciate you talking to me about this, but I'm going to keep talking to you about it. It's really important.
Yeah, I just don't see the problem in it right now and maybe it's because I haven't really had that traumatic of an experience but I'm...
Do you want to wait for that to happen? Do you want to wait for a dramatic experience?

You're right. I don't want to be too far gone before it's too late. Like I can imagine something possibly happening where it's to a degree where I can't escape. And I guess I've never really had any real experience where alcohol has really affected me that much or affected anybody close to me that much. So I guess it's something that I feel like I'm in control of but in reality I might not have as much control as I think.
Alright, well maybe it's something we can work on together and you know, I think we should come up with a plan that's going to work for you so that you can get control here and stop drinking.
Yeah, I think that would be a good step forward into a life of possibly being sober and just experiencing the true aspects of life rather than the haziness of alcohol.
Okay, sounds good.

I mainly when I puke or it's just the feeling that I get in my stomach if I drink too much, it's just very overwhelming.

Got it. So you're sort of testing and pushing it and sometimes crossing that limit and having some of the consequences that you mentioned before.
Yeah, just so I know how it feels now so that later on when the situation is more drastic and more out of control, I know what I can do or where my limit is at.

In terms of career wise?

I would love to travel. I would love to see the world for what it is. And I've always seen pictures and videos of how the world is, but I've never really experienced that. So getting a full experience is really important to you, it sounds like throughout your life. I guess it could interfere with allowing myself to feel the effects of living life to the fullest. But I wouldn't want to tamper with drinking too much often, just because I know I've seen the consequences that drinking has on people and I know that I would never want to get to a degree where I need to drink constantly every single day. I don't want to ever get to that point.

Okay. So just to kind of summarize what you've told me so far. You're drinking pretty regularly, but you are trying to limit yourself. You feel like three drinks maybe is probably the maximum that you can drink before you're having some of these negative consequences and you feel better if you limit yourself to three or less.
Yeah, I feel more in control.

And then kind of looking ahead, you don't want to find yourself being someone who's drinking all the time or someone who feels out of control with their drinking. You've seen that maybe in other people's lives and it's not appealing to you at all.
Not at all.
And you do have some big goals for your life that you want to achieve that drinking too much could also interfere with. So where do you think you want to go from here with regard to your drinking?

Maybe now that I know my limits to an extent, I kind of don't want to push it so much. Now that I know what I can do and where I can go, I would like to mitigate that as much as possible. I just want to have fun being me, but I don't want me to be influenced by alcohol so much. Like I want to live the sober life to an extent, but I know that alcohol is just going to tamper with that.

So for right now it feels like a reasonable goal for you would be to sort of limit your drinking and make sure you're stopping at three, for example, or maybe even limiting the number of times that you're drinking.

Yeah, or like not drinking in the mornings or just strictly for social purposes, just to not have it around. Like I don't want to have it in my fridge if my parents have it, I don't want to have to deal with that.
Okay. What do you see as some benefits to that?
Benefits in terms of...
...to sticking to those limits.

I guess I could definitely live a more fulfilled life to an extent. Like I could possibly be more productive, more efficient in my work and where I can possibly be in the next few years of my life. And I think that by not drinking it will definitely have a better effect on my life.
Yeah. Well, I think taking steps to limit and cut back on your drinking is a really good idea. I really appreciate you taking the time to talk with me about it and being open and honest.
My pleasure.
You know, if you don't mind, I would like to talk to you probably about this in a couple weeks or a couple months, just check in how things are going.
Right. Sounds good.
All right. Sounds good. Thank you very much.
Sure.

This time the youth minister began by expressing concern but relied on open questions and reflective listening to build rapport and encourage Tommy to share his experiences. The youth minister also encouraged Tommy to look ahead to consider how his drinking could affect his future plans. By exploring his values and relating them to his drinking, she developed a discrepancy between his future goals and his current behaviors, highlighting the need to make some adjustments to his drinking. Using a summary, the youth minister was able to transition smoothly to a discussion of options, and Tommy identified a realistic goal for himself that matched his values. As a result, he is much more likely to follow through on his plans and actually make a change in his drinking.

We're right at the point where the action happens. You aren't in the situation yet, but we're where the thoughts are being conceived. Can we slow down and just watch it? I want to do something odd to show how the mind works. I have a pen here that says something: 'woo.'
Yes, you do. It says woo.

Good catch. Let's do the same thing with that thought too. That segment was ACT consistent, using techniques to create separation between the person and their mind. Now let's look at an inconsistent example.

Hang on to that when the anxiety hits to remember these things aren't necessarily true. That segment was inconsistent because it focused on ridiculing the thoughts to make them go away, rather than just noticing them. Now we'll see a student struggling with career choices.

That was a 'normal' interaction but inconsistent with ACT because we focused on the content of the problem rather than the process. Now let's see a more consistent approach with the same client.
What's inside this choice? It feels like your thoughts are very close, almost blinding. Is that a familiar place for you?

Your mind is trying to help, but it's doing something very familiar. Let's notice what the mind is doing and what's showing up in your body. Every time you make a decision, your mind says you're leaving something behind, right?

It is scary when you open some doors and close others. Can you open up to that scariness rather than trying to fix it? You're not doing anything wrong; it's just part of the process.

In this section, we caught the 'mindy' process that pulls people into obsessive problem-solving and created some separation to allow for a more flexible way to explore life's choices.

At the end of the day, I suspect that would be less desirable to me than if I had a therapist who was also an expert on process but also had some felt experience of what I was going through. I think I would still feel happier about that. But I thought that Danielle showed sufficient authority and awareness of this issue and she was able to manage it in the moment for me to feel well, maybe that was worth another go. But my gut feeling would be that at some point or other we would hit this, we'd come back to this point again and this wouldn't be the only time we'd come here, there'd be moments where I'd be looking for some insight perhaps or some other perspective from someone who'd been there before. So I think what was done was good, it got us some of the way, but I think there'd be tests ahead of us.

Okay, so I've just finished being a therapist for Alf who presented as a man with midlife crisis type issues and was concerned that as a young therapist I wouldn't be able to understand his experiences because I haven't myself been through them. And I realized that going through life we can't experience every single thing and we're always going to have clients come in with something you haven't yourself been through. So I guess for me it was just about saying to myself I can still offer these people something and I can still help them. And I can at least I guess have some understanding and empathy for what they're going through, and I think that that is the most important thing. I feel that the therapy itself in that section went well, I think we came to a point where we could perhaps leave that issue aside for now and progress further, and with that in mind constantly as a therapist, the process then being trying to illustrate to him all the time empathy through my reflection of his feelings all the time to show him I guess that I can get it, or if I don't, at least asking him and checking in with him to see whether I'm on the right path. It was confronting as a therapist and it probably always will be, you have that slight kind of your heart flutters a little bit because you feel like you're being challenged. I think the most important thing for me was to not react to that in a defensive way and try and justify myself to him but to really focus on what was going on for him, which I think started off a nice modelling of that this is always going to be what's going on for him and I'll always be wanting to know that. So whatever comes up for him and he feels that I don't understand, that was a nice starting point for him.

In that segment, I was playing the client. I'd been telling my therapist about my achievements and felt pleased, but when the topic shifted to my son, I sensed all was not well. I felt unfairly challenged in my decision-making, which is not a comfortable situation for a client to be in.

I can imagine how he'd feel. He's a teenager trying to break away from parents and get some freedom.
The way they describe Tim is that he is also a very anxious boy. I'm wondering if he might even be relieved if his parents say he can't go.

I must say that it's almost as though you've decided that this is how Tim has to feel. I'm wondering whether your own strength of feeling about this issue is interfering with your ability to be objective.

In terms of what it's like for Tim or for you?
